At L33, the agent identified the alignment issue: with cols % 8 != 0, later row pointers may not be 16-byte aligned. It rewrote the span helpers so each row segment aligns its own pointer before using 8-element vector accesses. The key strategy in scan_span was:

uintptr_t addr = reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(p0);
uintptr_t aligned_addr = (addr + 15) & ~uintptr_t(15);
p_aligned = reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat16*>(aligned_addr);
if (p_aligned > p1) p_aligned = p1;

int head = static_cast<int>(p_aligned - p0);
...
int vec_elems = static_cast<int>(p1 - p_aligned);
int nvec = vec_elems / 8;
...
int tail_start = head + nvec * 8;
int tail = (end - start) - tail_start;

The same head/vector/tail approach was applied in write_span, aligning the output pointer by the matching offset from the input pointer. This allows scalar accesses at the front and end while keeping each uint4 access aligned.

// Block reduce; result valid in thread 0.
__device__ __forceinline__ MD block_reduce_md_t0(MD v, MD* smem, int tid, int nwarps) {
    int lane = tid & 31;
    int warp = tid >> 5;
    v = warp_reduce_md(v);
    if (lane == 0) smem[warp] = v;
    __syncthreads();
    v = (tid < nwarps) ? smem[tid] : md_init();
    if (warp == 0) v = warp_reduce_md(v);
    return v;

The reconstructed final solution uses load_inline to compile a real CUDA C++ BF16 kernel. Relevant prior context

An initial vectorized kernel failed numeric stress checks with a misaligned-address error. The fix added scalar handling before and after the 16-byte-aligned body for rows with unaligned starts or tails, including the 4127-column case. A shared-memory single-pass experiment was slower; Nsight Compute showed the two-pass path reaching about 86–92% DRAM while the shared-memory version reached about 47%. PTX streaming stores also regressed, so the final solution retained regular stores.

For rows that need more parallelism, the implementation splits work across blocks, merges each segment’s online (m, d) state, and writes output by segment. It uses 128, 256, or 512 threads per block based on row width. The final version also applies a persisting L2 access-policy window to the input, up to 64 MiB, to help the write pass reuse input data.

The core stable merge is:

r.m = fmaxf(a.m, b.m);
float ea = (a.d == 0.f) ? 0.f : __expf(a.m - r.m);
float eb = (b.d == 0.f) ? 0.f : __expf(b.m - r.m);
r.d = a.d * ea + b.d * eb;

The fast path uses 8 BF16 values per 16-byte load/store, with scalar handling for alignment and tails. BF16 inputs are converted to FP32 for reductions and exponentiation, then rounded back to BF16.
